understanding.emotion: heartbroken and unable to let go
understanding.bridge: What you are living with is what the texts call not feeling good enough, and that is where this week begins.

week_beats.hook: You recognise the ache and the replaying, named without blame.
week_beats.diagnose: You see that grief is love with nowhere to go, and that is why the heart aches.
week_beats.steady: You hold that what is real in you cannot be taken, and both the love and the ending can be true.
week_beats.act: You try one act of letting the heart feel, and one act of turning away from the story.
week_beats.story: A woman who loved and was left shows you that grief is love with nowhere to go, and that you can survive it.

understanding.core_struggle: Her three-year relationship ended with a single text, and now she cannot stop watching his story and wondering if she is going mad.
understanding.mirror: Three years, one text, and now the story you cannot look away from.
understanding.insight: You are not going mad. You are grieving a real bond that ended by a text, and the mind will not let it rest until it is named.

queries.hook: The ache of a love that was real and has now ended, and the mind that will not stop replaying the moment it left.
queries.diagnose: Grief is love with nowhere to go; everything that comes together must part, and the heart aches because the bond was real.
queries.steady: What is real in you cannot be taken; the love was real, the ending was real, and both can be true at once.
queries.act: Let the heart feel what it feels, and let the mind rest; do not watch the story again today, and write down what the bond gave you.
queries.story: A woman who loved deeply and was left by a single text, who learned that grief is love with nowhere to go, and found her footing again.

weeks: Grief is love with nowhere to go

verse.speaker: Arjuna
verse.setting: Arjuna confesses the mind is as hard to hold as the wind; Krishna answers.
verse.sanskrit: चञ्चलं हि मनः कृष्ण प्रमाथि बलवद्दृढम् । तस्याहं निग्रहं मन्ये वायोरिव सुदुष्करम् ॥
verse.line: The mind is restless, stormy, stubborn and strong. Holding it feels like holding the wind.
verse.translation: For the mind is restless, Krishna, turbulent, powerful and stubborn. I think it is as hard to hold as the wind.
verse.why: The mind is hard to hold, but practice and letting go train it.

prasang.title: Mastering the mind
prasang.summary: Arjuna says the mind is restless, stormy and stubborn. Krishna agrees, and says practice and letting go can train it.
prasang.lesson: The mind is hard to hold, but practice and letting go train it.

verse.meaning: Arjuna is on the battlefield, looking at the faces of the men he must fight. He tells Krishna that the mind is restless, turbulent and stubborn. It is as hard to hold as the wind. Krishna does not tell him to stop thinking. He says the mind can be trained by practice and by letting go.
verse.for_you: You are watching his story and wondering if you are losing your mind. That is not madness. That is a heart that cannot yet accept a door that was slammed shut. The mind is not your enemy. It is simply holding on to a bond that mattered.
verse.try_today: Watch the story once, then close the app.
verse.scene_line: You are standing in a field, staring at a wind that will not hold still.
asks: How do I stop the mind from replaying one message?
Is this storm in my head a sign of weakness?
How do I let go when the bond was real?

verse.speaker: Kausalya
verse.setting: After lashing out at Dasharatha over Ram's exile, Kausalya apologises and explains what grief did to her.
verse.sanskrit: शोको नाशयते धैर्यं शोको नाशयते श्रुतम्। शोको नाशयते सर्वं नास्ति शोकसमो रिपुः॥
verse.line: Grief wears away your steadiness and your judgement. There is no enemy like it.
verse.translation: Grief destroys steadiness, grief destroys learning, grief destroys everything. There is no enemy like grief.
verse.why: Grief makes us wound those we love; apologising quickly heals more than being right.
verse.misuse: Not a ban on grieving; a warning not to let sorrow make your decisions.

prasang.title: Kausalya's reproach and apology
prasang.summary: In her grief Kausalya lashes out at her husband for exiling their son. When he folds his hands and asks her forgiveness, she is horrified, apologises, and explains that grief made her speak.
prasang.story_hook: She said the words; then she saw her husband fold his hands to her.
prasang.lesson: Grief makes us wound those we love; apologising quickly heals more than being right.

verse.meaning: Kausalya, Ram's mother, has just lashed out at Dasharatha for exiling their son. Seeing him fold his hands and ask for her forgiveness, she is horrified at her own words. She tells him that grief has worn away her steadiness and her judgement, and that there is no enemy quite like it. She explains that sorrow can make us wound those we love, and that offering an apology quickly heals more than holding onto being right.
verse.for_you: That single text left your mind spinning, and now you are watching his story on loop. The grief is not the madness. It is love with nowhere to go. Kausalya wounded her husband because sorrow took her steadiness, and you are feeling that same pull.
verse.try_today: Notice the moment you reach for the phone and pause.

verse.speaker: Bhartrihari
verse.setting: Closing verse of the section on steadfastness.
verse.sanskrit: छिन्नोऽपि रोहति तरुश्चन्द्रः क्षीणोऽपि वर्धते लोके । इति विमृशन्तः सन्तः सन्तप्यन्ते न लोकेऽस्मिन् ॥
verse.line: A cut tree grows back; the waning moon fills again. Remembering this, the wise do not despair.
verse.translation: A tree that is cut grows again; the waning moon waxes again in the world. Reflecting on this, the good are not tormented in this world.
verse.why: Setbacks rarely last for those who keep going on the right path.

prasang.title: Nitishatakam: On steadfastness
prasang.summary: Steadfastness: the gods kept churning the ocean past jewels and poison until they found nectar; the steady do not leave the right path whatever people say. A struck ball bounces back and a cut tree grows again.
prasang.lesson: Setbacks rarely last for those who keep going on the right path.

verse.meaning: Bhartrihari speaks to the reader at the close of his thoughts on standing firm. He says that a tree cut down will grow back, and the moon that wanes will fill again in the world. Reflecting on this, the wise do not despair. He is saying that setbacks rarely last for those who keep going on the right path. The mind is restless, stormy, stubborn and strong. Holding it feels like holding the wind. But what is real in you cannot be taken.
verse.for_you: You are sitting in the quiet after the text, watching his story again and again, and wondering if you are losing your mind. You are not. The mind will not let it rest until it is named. What is real in you cannot be taken.
verse.try_today: Notice one small sign of life around you, like a plant or a cloud, and let it sit with you.
verse.scene_line: You are in your own waiting room, watching the moon wane.
asks: How do I know my steadiness is still here?
How do I stop checking his story without judging myself?
How do I hold the wind without breaking?

verse.speaker: Ashtavakra
verse.setting: King Janaka asks the young sage Ashtavakra how a person becomes free.
verse.sanskrit: त्वया व्याप्तमिदं विश्वं त्वयि प्रोतं यथार्थतः । शुद्धबुद्धस्वरूपस्त्वं मा गमः क्षुद्रचित्तताम् ॥
verse.line: You are pure awareness, wider than any worry. Don't let your mind shrink into pettiness.
verse.translation: This whole universe is pervaded by you and strung on you. By nature you are pure awareness; do not fall into smallness of mind.
verse.why: You are more than your roles and worries; freedom starts with how you see yourself.

prasang.title: Janaka asks the boy-sage how to be free
prasang.summary: King Janaka, ruler of Mithila, asks the young sage Ashtavakra three questions: how to gain wisdom, freedom and dispassion. Ashtavakra answers at once: you are not the body or your roles but the awareness that watches them, and freedom is available now.
prasang.story_hook: A powerful king bowed before a boy whose body was bent in eight places, and asked him how to be free.
prasang.lesson: You are more than your roles and worries; freedom starts with how you see yourself.

verse.meaning: King Janaka sits before the young sage Ashtavakra. The king asks how a person becomes free. Ashtavakra replies that this whole universe is strung on you. By nature you are pure awareness. Do not fall into smallness of mind. He means you are the space where the breakup and the grief appear. The pain is real, but it does not shrink who you are. Freedom is not a future prize. It is seeing yourself as the watcher, not the wound.
verse.for_you: You are watching his story over and over, waiting for a sign. That is the smallness of mind. It is not weakness. It is the mind trying to prove the bond was real. You can hold the love and the ending at the same time.
verse.try_today: When you want to check his story, name the feeling out loud. Just say it.
verse.scene_line: You are the king asking how to be free while the story of your bond plays out.
asks: How do I hold the love and the ending together?

verse.speaker: Dharmavyadha (the righteous meat-seller)
verse.setting: In Mithila, a meat-seller famed for wisdom teaches a proud ascetic what goodness really is.
verse.sanskrit: यत्कल्याणमभिध्यायेत्तत्रात्मानं नियोजयेत् / न पापं प्रति पापः स्यात्साधुरेव सदा भवेत्
verse.line: Don't become bad because someone was bad to you. Stay good.
verse.translation: Keep your mind on what is good and commit yourself to it. Do not become wicked in return for wickedness; always remain good.
verse.why: Wisdom lives in ordinary people doing ordinary work honestly. Care for your parents.
verse.misuse: Staying good does not mean staying silent or unprotected.

matched.label: I can't let go of resentment

prasang.title: Vyadha Gita: the butcher who taught a sage
prasang.summary: A proud ascetic, Kaushika, is sent to learn from a meat-seller in Mithila. The butcher teaches him plain goodness: don't return evil, repent and resolve, keep envy away, care for your parents, and don't spend your one life making enemies.
prasang.lesson: Wisdom lives in ordinary people doing ordinary work honestly. Care for your parents.

verse.for_you: Be on your own side: lift yourself up, make amends where you can, and begin again; no one who does good is lost.

verse.speaker: Vidula
verse.setting: Queen Vidula rouses her son, who lies defeated and despairing after losing his kingdom.
verse.sanskrit: माऽऽत्मानमवमन्यस्व मैनमल्पेन बीभरः / मनः कृत्वा सुकल्याणं मा भैस्त्वं प्रतिसंहर
verse.line: Don't think less of yourself or settle for little. Set your mind on something good, and stop fearing.
verse.translation: Do not hold yourself in contempt, and do not keep it going on too little. Set your mind on what is truly good; don't be afraid. Pull yourself together.
verse.why: Past failure doesn't define you. Results are uncertain, but those who never try never succeed.

prasang.title: Vidula rouses her defeated son
prasang.summary: Kunti sends Yudhishthira the old story of Queen Vidula, who finds her son lying defeated after losing his kingdom. She shames, then reasons, then encourages him until he rises and fights for it again.
prasang.story_hook: A prince lay in bed after losing everything, until his mother walked in and refused to let him stay there.
prasang.lesson: Past failure doesn't define you. Results are uncertain, but those who never try never succeed.

verse.for_you: Be on your own side as the self is on yours; make amends, learn, and begin again without carrying the old verdict.

story.title: Pingala's song: the night she stopped waiting
story.story_hook: Pingala sat awake listening for footsteps that never came, until she stopped listening.
story.summary: Pingala waited all night for a lover who never came. At last she saw that her peace depended on someone else's arrival, let the expectation go, and slept peacefully.
story.lesson: Letting go of an expectation can bring the sleep that waiting never will.

anchor.speaker: Pingala (quoted by Bhishma)
anchor.setting: Pingala, left waiting all night by a lover who never came, finally lets go and finds peace.
anchor.sanskrit: सुखं निराशः स्वपिति नैराश्यं परमं सुखम् / आशामनाशां कृत्वा हि सुखं स्वपिति पिङ्गला
anchor.line: Pingala let go of her expectation and slept peacefully. Letting go of expectation is the greatest ease.
anchor.translation: The one free of expectation sleeps in peace; freedom from expectation is the highest happiness. Turning hope into no-hope, Pingala sleeps peacefully.
anchor.why: Letting go of an expectation can bring the sleep that waiting never will.
anchor.misuse: This is about clinging to an outcome, not about giving up hope in life.

prasang.title: Pingala's song: the night she stopped waiting
prasang.summary: Pingala waited all night for a lover who never came. At last she saw that her peace depended on someone else's arrival, let the expectation go, and slept peacefully.
prasang.story_hook: Pingala sat awake listening for footsteps that never came, until she stopped listening.
prasang.lesson: Letting go of an expectation can bring the sleep that waiting never will.

story.hook_title: Pingala waited all night for a man who never came
story.teaser: Pingala waited all night for a man who never came
story.for_you: The story of Pingala is about you. She sat awake all night waiting for a man who never came, her heart breaking with each passing hour. Then she saw that her peace was tied to someone else's choice. She let the waiting go and finally slept.
asks: What is the smallest thing I can let go of tonight?
How do I sleep when the heart still wants to check?
Can I let the waiting go without letting him go?
